opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting challenge, because Gemini is a genuinely enormous collaborative effort. There are hundreds of people, really more than a thousand if you count everyone, contributing across pre-training, post-training, infrastructure, data, evaluations, serving, safety, and all the product integrations. So you can't just have one small group making every decision.

The way we've tried to structure it is to break the work into areas with clear owners. There's a pre-training effort, a post-training effort, people focused on particular capabilities like coding, multimodal, long context, or reasoning, and teams working on the infrastructure that makes all of it run. Each area has leads who are responsible for driving progress there and figuring out which ideas are ready to go into the next model.

One thing that's been really important is a fairly disciplined process for deciding what goes into a big training run. People are exploring lots of ideas at smaller scale, and we want that creativity and bottom-up exploration. But when you're about to commit an enormous amount of compute to a large run, you want good evidence that each change actually helps, and that the changes compose well together. So there's a lot of work on small-scale experiments and scaling studies, with checkpoints where we look at the results and decide which ideas graduate to the next scale.

Communication is the other big piece. We're spread across many locations and time zones, from Mountain View and the Bay Area to London, Zurich, New York, Bangalore, and elsewhere. So we rely a lot on written communication: design docs, shared result summaries, and very active chat spaces where people post experiment results and discuss them. Having that information flow openly means someone working on one piece can see what's happening elsewhere and spot connections, or problems, early.

Honestly, it's not perfect. With that many people there's always some overhead, and you have to balance letting people move quickly and independently against keeping everyone pointed in roughly the same direction. But I think the payoff of pooling people and compute into one coherent effort, rather than several competing ones, has been really significant. It lets us build a much better model than any one subgroup could alone.

r001.rationale: The response calls coordinating Gemini’s large contributor base a challenging organizational effort and explains how shared processes help contributors’ work fit together and improve the resulting model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a big group. Gemini at this point involves hundreds, honestly thousands of people across Google DeepMind and other parts of Google, and a lot of them are in different time zones, so you can't just put everyone in a room. The way I think about it is that you want a fairly small number of people who have a clear picture of the overall direction, and then you want to decompose the problem into pieces that teams can own and make progress on somewhat independently, while still having good ways to recombine the pieces.

So concretely, there are areas like pretraining, data, post-training, evaluation, infrastructure, serving, long context, multimodal, and each of those has a group of people who are the experts and who are trying to push that frontier. The thing that ties it together is a shared sense of what the next model needs to be, and a pretty strong evaluation culture. If someone has an idea, whether it's an architectural tweak or a new data mixture or a new way of doing RL, the question is always, can you show it works at a small scale, does it scale, and does it hold up when you combine it with the other things people are doing. Because one of the hard parts is that a bunch of improvements that each look good in isolation don't necessarily stack. So you need a process for integrating them and checking that the whole is actually better.

The other piece is communication. We lean heavily on things like shared docs, a lot of asynchronous discussion, and regular syncs where the leads of the different areas get together and look at where we are versus where we expected to be. I personally spend a lot of time reading. Reading experiment reports, reading chat threads, looking at eval dashboards. That's how you notice that two groups are solving the same problem in different ways, or that something that one team learned would be really useful to another team.

And then infrastructure matters a lot for coordination, more than people think. If you have a common codebase, common training infrastructure, common eval tooling, then a researcher in London and a researcher in Mountain View can actually build on each other's work instead of reinventing things. A lot of the leverage comes from making it easy for a good idea to go from one person's experiment to something that's in the next big training run.

I've always liked working on things where there's a clear, ambitious goal that a lot of people care about, because that goal does a lot of the coordination for you. People will self-organize around it. Your job is mostly to keep the picture clear, remove obstacles, and make sure the right people are talking to each other.

r001.rationale: The response describes coordinating hundreds or thousands of Gemini contributors as difficult, explaining that teams must integrate their work because improvements that look good alone may not combine. It presents coordination as a way to make teams’ contributions build on one another and improve the overall model.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to give people a shared direction without trying to centrally manage every experiment. Building these models involves a lot of different kinds of work: data, training infrastructure, model architecture, evaluation, and getting the resulting system to work well for users. Those pieces are very connected, so people need to understand how their work affects the rest of the effort.

You want smaller teams to have enough autonomy to explore ideas, but you also need clear ways to evaluate those ideas and bring the promising ones together. Something can look good in a small experiment and then turn out not to help at the scale you care about. Having shared evaluations and communicating results—including things that didn’t work—helps everyone make better decisions.

And then there’s a balance between exploration and execution. You want to keep pursuing new approaches, while also being able to say, okay, for this training run, here’s what we’re going to do. That gives people a concrete target without shutting down the research that might make the next model better.

r001.rationale: The response describes coordinating many contributors and connected workstreams through shared direction, evaluation, and integration so their work improves the resulting model. Its discussion of balancing team autonomy, exploration, and execution conveys the organizational challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to give people a clear sense of what we’re trying to accomplish, while leaving room for teams to figure out how best to contribute. Building a model like Gemini involves a lot of interconnected work: data, training infrastructure, model architecture, evaluation, and getting the model into products. Those pieces have to fit together.

You want to break the work into areas where people can make progress independently, but also have frequent communication about what they’re learning and where the dependencies are. If someone improves the efficiency of the training system, that can change which experiments the research team can afford to run. And if an evaluation reveals a weakness, that needs to feed back into the data and modeling work.

So it’s a balance between having a shared direction and enabling lots of experimentation. You don’t want every decision to go through one person. You want people close to the work to make good decisions, with enough shared context that those decisions add up to a better model.

r001.rationale: The response describes coordinating many contributors across interconnected Gemini work, managing dependencies and feedback so their efforts combine into a better model. Its emphasis on balancing shared direction, independent progress, and decentralized decisions conveys the organizational challenge.
